    "# Matplotlib - Numpy images\n",
    "\n",
    "## [Download exercises zip](../_static/generated/visualization.zip)\n",
    "\n",
    "Images are a direct application of matrices, and show we can nicely translate a numpy matrix cell into a pixel on the screen.\n",
    "\n",
    "Typically, images are divided into color channels: a common scheme is the RGB model, which stands for Red Green and Blue. In this tutorial we will load an image where each pixel is made of three integer values ranging from 0 to 255 included. Each integer indicates how much of a color component is present in the pixel, with zero meaning absence and 255 bright colors."
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "markdown",
   "metadata": {},
   "source": [

    "\n",
    "**NOTE 2**: We are still talking about matrices, so pictures also follow the very same conventions of regular algebra we've also seen with lists of lists:  the first index is for rows and starts from 0 in the left upper corner, and second index is for columns.\n",
    "\n",
    "**NOTE 3**: the indeces shown on the extracted picture are _not_ the indeces of the original matrix!"

    "## Writing into images\n",
    "\n",
    "Let's go back to images. First note that `gimg` was generated by calling `pt.imshow`, which set it as READ-ONLY:"
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "markdown",
   "metadata": {},
   "source": [
    "```python\n",
    "gimg[0,0] = 255  # NOT POSSIBLE WITH LOADED IMAGES!\n",
    "---------------------------------------------------------------------------\n",
    "ValueError                                Traceback (most recent call last)\n",
    "<ipython-input-186-7d21dd84cac2> in <module>()\n",
    "----> 1 img[0,0,0] = 4  # NOT POSSIBLE!\n",
    "\n",
    "ValueError: assignment destination is read-only\n",
    "```"
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "markdown",
   "metadata": {},
   "source": [
    "If we want something we can write into, we need to perform a **deep copy**:"
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "code",
   "execution_count": 29,
   "metadata": {},
   "outputs": [
    {
     "data": {
      "text/plain": [
       "255"
      ]
     },
     "execution_count": 29,
     "metadata": {},
     "output_type": "execute_result"
    }
   ],
   "source": [
    "mimg = gimg.copy()  # *DEEP* COPY\n",
    "mimg[0,0] = 255  # the copy is writable\n",
    "mimg[0,0]"
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "markdown",

   "cell_type": "markdown",
   "metadata": {},
   "source": [
    "Why do we get values less than < 100 ?? \n",
    "\n",
    "This is not so weird, technically it's called integer overflow and is the way CPU works with byte sized integers, so most programming languages actually behave like this. In regular Python you don't notice it because standard Python allows for arbitrary sized integers, but that comes at a big  performance cost that Numpy cannot afford, so in a sense we can say Numpy is 'closer to the metal' of the CPU.\n",
    "\n",
    "Let's see a simpler example:"
   ]
  },
  {

    "### Exercise - Be bright\n",

    "Now try writing some code which enhances scene luminosity by adding `light=125` without distortions (you may still see some pixellation due to the fact we have taken just one color channel from the original image)\n",
    "\n",
    "* **DO NOT** exceed 255 value for cells - if you see dark spots in your image where before there was white (i.e. background sky), it means color cycled back to small values!\n",

    "* **MUST** have unsigned bytes as cells type\n",

    "## Exercise - Beyond the limit\n",
    "\n",
    "... weird things happen:"
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "code",
   "execution_count": 78,
   "metadata": {},
   "outputs": [
    {
     "data": {
      "text/plain": [
       "<matplotlib.image.AxesImage at 0x7ff57ec72b50>"
      ]
     },
     "execution_count": 78,
     "metadata": {},
     "output_type": "execute_result"
    },
    {
     "data": {
      "image/png": "",
      "text/plain": [
       "<Figure size 432x288 with 1 Axes>"
      ]
     },
     "metadata": {
      "needs_background": "light"
     },
     "output_type": "display_data"
    }
   ],
   "source": [
    "plt.imshow(img + 10)"
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "code",
   "execution_count": 79,
   "metadata": {},
   "outputs": [
    {
     "data": {
      "text/plain": [
       "255"
      ]
     },
     "execution_count": 79,
     "metadata": {},
     "output_type": "execute_result"
    }
   ],
   "source": [
    "mimg = img.copy()\n",
    "mimg[0,0,0] = 255  # limit !!\n",
    "mimg[0,0,0]"
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "code",
   "execution_count": 80,
   "metadata": {},
   "outputs": [],
   "source": [
    "mimg[0,0,0] += 1   # integer overflow, cycles back - note it does not happen in regular Python !"
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "code",
   "execution_count": 81,
   "metadata": {},
   "outputs": [
    {
     "data": {
      "text/plain": [
       "0"
      ]
     },
     "execution_count": 81,
     "metadata": {},
     "output_type": "execute_result"
    }
   ],
   "source": [
    "mimg[0,0,0]         "
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "markdown",
   "metadata": {},
   "source": [
    "Note this is not so weird, technically this is called overflow and us the way CPU works with byte sized integers, so most programming languages actually behave like this.\n",
    "\n",
    "You can get the same problem when subtracting:"
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "code",
   "execution_count": 82,
   "metadata": {},
   "outputs": [
    {
     "data": {
      "text/plain": [
       "255"
      ]
     },
     "execution_count": 82,
     "metadata": {},
     "output_type": "execute_result"
    }
   ],
   "source": [
    "mimg[0,0,0] = 0     # limit !!\n",
    "mimg[0,0,0] -= 1    # integer overflow , cycles forward\n",
    "mimg[0,0,0]"
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "code",
   "execution_count": 83,
   "metadata": {
    "scrolled": true
   },
   "outputs": [
    {
     "data": {
      "text/plain": [
       "<matplotlib.image.AxesImage at 0x7ff57ebef550>"
      ]
     },
     "execution_count": 83,
     "metadata": {},
     "output_type": "execute_result"
    },
    {
     "data": {
      "image/png": "",
      "text/plain": [
       "<Figure size 432x288 with 1 Axes>"
      ]
     },
     "metadata": {
      "needs_background": "light"
     },
     "output_type": "display_data"
    }
   ],
   "source": [
    "plt.imshow(img + img)"
   ]
  },
